title: Separating Mixtures
subtitle: After-lab quiz
intro: Answer from what you saw in the lab this week. This is a self-check — read the feedback at the end, that's the useful part.

questions.stem: You have muddy water — sand mixed into water. Which method separates the sand from the water?
questions.misconception: Choosing evaporation here means they're reaching for the 'salt water' method without asking whether the solid is dissolved.

options.why: Sand does not dissolve, so its grains stay much bigger than the holes in filter paper. The water passes through and the sand is trapped.

Evaporation would work eventually, but you'd lose all the water as vapour and wait a long time. It's the method for dissolved solids — sand isn't dissolved, so filtering is faster and keeps the water.
Distillation separates liquids from dissolved substances by boiling and condensing. Sand isn't dissolved, so all that boiling equipment is doing a job filter paper does in seconds.
Magnets only attract magnetic materials like iron. Sand is mostly silica (quartz), which a magnet ignores completely.

questions.stem: You want to get the salt back out of salty water. Which method works?
questions.misconception: Filtration answers here mean the student hasn't grasped that dissolved particles are far smaller than filter-paper pores — the 'dissolving means disappearing into tiny pieces' idea hasn't landed.

options.why: Dissolved salt breaks up into particles far too small for filter paper to catch — they wash straight through with the water. If you filtered salty water, you'd just get salty water in the beaker underneath.
Heating the salty water makes the water leave as vapour. The salt can't evaporate at these temperatures, so it's left behind as crystals in the dish.
Decanting means carefully pouring liquid off a settled solid. Dissolved salt never settles — it's spread evenly through the water — so there's nothing to pour the water off from.
Chromatography separates mixtures of dyes or inks by how far they travel up paper. It can't collect salt for you — and the goal here is to get the salt back, not to see what's in the mixture.

questions.stem: This time you want the pure water from salty water — and you want to keep it. Which method?
questions.misconception: Evaporation answers show the student remembers 'heat the salt water' but hasn't noticed the water escapes. The keep-the-salt vs keep-the-water distinction is the point of this question.

options.why: So close — but in an open dish the water escapes into the air as vapour. You'd keep the salt and lose exactly the thing you wanted.

Distillation boils the water into vapour, then cools the vapour in a condenser so it turns back into liquid water and drips into a clean container. The salt stays behind in the flask — you keep both, but especially the pure water.
Dissolved salt particles are far smaller than the holes in filter paper, so they pass straight through with the water. The water coming out is just as salty as the water going in.
Freezing salty water gives you salty ice — the salt is trapped among the ice crystals, not separated out. (Partial freezing can concentrate salt, but it doesn't give you pure water.)

questions.misconception: Options b and d both signal a 'the paper does something active/chemical' model instead of a simple particle-size model.

options.text: The undissolved solid's particles are too big to fit through the tiny holes in the filter paper.
options.why: That's the whole trick. Filter paper is full of tiny holes — liquid particles and dissolved particles fit through; grains of undissolved solid don't. It's a sieve, just a very fine one.

options.text: The filter paper soaks up the liquid and leaves the solid behind.
options.why: The paper gets wet, but the liquid isn't absorbed and stored in it — it passes through the holes and is collected underneath. If paper worked by soaking, the liquid would be gone, not in your beaker.

options.text: The solid dissolves into the filter paper.
options.why: Solids don't dissolve into paper — dissolving happens into a liquid (a solvent). The solid sits on top of the paper as the residue; you can see it there at the end.

options.text: The filter paper is chemically attracted to solids.
options.why: No chemistry is happening — filtration is purely physical. The paper doesn't attract anything; it just has holes smaller than the solid's grains.

questions.stem: You've spilled iron filings into sulfur powder. What's the easiest way to separate them?

options.why: Iron is magnetic and sulfur is not. Run a magnet (in a plastic bag, so the filings come off easily) over the mixture and the iron jumps out, leaving the sulfur behind.
Neither iron nor sulfur dissolves in water, so filtering just gives you the same mixture back — now wet. Filtration only separates things when one part passes through and the other doesn't.
Evaporation removes a liquid from a mixture. There's no liquid here — two dry powders — so there's nothing to evaporate.

options.text: Pick the iron out with tweezers
options.why: You could, in theory — but filings are tiny and there are thousands of them. The question asks for the easiest way, and a magnet does the whole job in seconds. Choosing a method means choosing the property that makes it fast.

questions.stem: What does paper chromatography tell you about a black ink?
questions.misconception: Students choosing c think chromatography is a purification method rather than an analysis method — worth separating 'finding out what's in it' from 'getting something back'.

options.text: Whether the ink is a mixture of different dyes, because each dye travels a different distance up the paper.
options.why: Each dye sticks to the paper and dissolves in the solvent by a different amount, so each one stops at a different height. One ink spot spreading into several colours proves the 'black' was really a mixture.
Chromatography says nothing about mass — for that you'd use a balance. It separates the parts of a mixture so you can see them.

options.text: It lets you collect large amounts of each dye to reuse.
options.why: The separated dyes end up as faint smears on paper — far too little to collect and reuse. Chromatography is for finding out what's in a mixture, not for getting the parts back in useful amounts.
Magnetism is tested with a magnet, and inks aren't magnetic anyway. Chromatography works on how well things dissolve and stick to paper — nothing to do with magnets.

questions.stem: Sand has settled at the bottom of a beaker of water. You carefully pour the water off the top without disturbing the sand. What is this called?

options.why: Decanting is exactly this: letting a solid settle, then pouring the liquid off the top. It's quick but rough — some water stays with the sand, which is why you'd filter if you needed a cleaner separation.

Distilling involves boiling a liquid and condensing its vapour — heating equipment, a condenser, the lot. Pouring water off settled sand needs none of that; similar-sounding word, very different method.
Dissolving is when a substance spreads out into a liquid and seems to disappear, like salt into water. The sand here has done the opposite — it's sitting visibly on the bottom.
Evaporating means the liquid leaves as vapour, usually with heating. Here the water is being poured away as a liquid, not turned into gas.

questions.stem: Why can mixtures be separated by methods like filtering and evaporating, when compounds can't?
questions.misconception: Wrong answers here usually mean the mixture/compound distinction itself is shaky — worth revisiting before the next topic, since ionic bonding builds on it.

options.text: In a mixture the substances are not chemically joined, so physical methods can pull them apart.
options.why: The parts of a mixture keep their own properties (sand is still sand, water is still water), and no chemical bonds hold them together — so differences like particle size, boiling point or magnetism can be used to separate them.

options.text: Mixtures are always liquids, and liquids are easy to separate.
options.why: Mixtures can be solids (iron and sulfur powders), liquids, or gases (air is a mixture). Being a liquid isn't what makes something separable — the lack of chemical bonds between the parts is.

options.text: Compounds are too heavy to separate.
options.why: Weight has nothing to do with it. Compounds resist physical separation because their elements are chemically bonded — you'd need a chemical reaction (like electrolysis) to split them, however light they are.

options.text: Mixtures always contain water, which helps them separate.
options.why: Plenty of mixtures contain no water at all — air, or iron filings and sulfur. What makes mixtures separable is that their parts aren't chemically joined, not the presence of water.

questions.stem: In salty water, what do we call the salt?
questions.misconception: Solute/solvent swaps are common and harmless-looking, but they cause real confusion when concentration calculations arrive in Year 11 — worth a two-minute drill.

options.why: The solute is the substance that dissolves — here, the salt. It dissolves into the solvent (the water), and together they make a solution.

The solvent is the liquid doing the dissolving — in salty water, that's the water. The salt is the thing being dissolved, which makes it the solute. The two words are easy to swap; 'solvent does the dissolving' is the anchor.
The solution is the whole finished mixture — salt and water together. The salt on its own is just one ingredient of it: the solute.
Residue is the solid left sitting on the filter paper after filtering. Dissolved salt passes through filter paper, so it never becomes a residue — it's the solute in the solution.

questions.stem: After filtering muddy water, what is the liquid that collects in the beaker underneath called?

options.why: The filtrate is whatever passes through the filter — here, the water. Easy to remember: the filtrATE is what went strAIGHT through.
The residue is the solid trapped on the filter paper — the mud, in this case. It resides (stays put) on the paper; the liquid below has a different name: the filtrate.
Solvent is a solutions word — the liquid that dissolves a solute. Mud doesn't dissolve in water, so this isn't a solution, and the collected liquid gets its filtering name instead: the filtrate.
A precipitate is a solid that forms during a chemical reaction in a solution. Nothing reacted here, and the thing collected is a liquid — it's the filtrate.
